newsitem.title: FRANCE: Knives out in row over modern French cuisine.
newsitem.headline: Knives out in row over modern French cuisine.

text.p: France's celebrity chefs are drawing their knives in a dispute over whether modern cuisine has betrayed traditional recipes and become an unappetising mish-mash.

Marc Veyrat, head of the top-rated Auberge Eridan restaurant in southeastern France, said on Thursday he was one of "at least 20 chefs" resigning from the Chamber of French Haute Cuisine with grievances, including the body's hostility to innovation.
"To get back to the roots of any tradition we need creativity, new influences. It's the same in architecture, music or any form of art," Veyrat told Reuters.
Chamber president Georges Blanc played down the dissent as a storm in a cognac glass. "The number of resignations is closer to 10 than to 20," he said.

"We have to stop these sterile rivalries. No one has an interest in fanning rows in the media, it damages the image of French cuisine," Blanc added. "I'd like them to come back to end this internal crisis."

The row has been simmering in the kitchens of France's most famous restaurants since May, when a dozen chefs, including Blanc and Alain Ducasse, issued a warning about an insidious slide towards indigestibility.
"A great dish is not a hodge-podge...True French cooking draws its strength and legitimacy from its history, our regions, our products and the unique French character," they said.
"We are alarmed to see the tendency among some who want to mix anything with everything on a plate to give the illusion of innovation at any price."

The left-leaning daily newspaper Liberation said that about 20 chefs, including at least seven with the coveted three-star rating in the red-bound Michelin Guide, were sending resignations to the Chamber to protest against Blanc's leadership.
"We chose freedom against those who choose cash...or power. If somebody wants to eat oysters with red wine, who has the right to stop them?" asked Marc Meneau, one of the dissidents.
The two sides, with innovators known as "leftists" pitted against "conservative" purists, struck a pact to "respect diversity" at a meeting three weeks ago.
Asked whether he had any regrets after signing the May declaration, Blanc said that he had done so "on an individual basis...I don't understand why the Chamber is getting mixed up in this."
He said that he hoped to finish his three-year term as head of the Chamber in the spring.
But Veyrat, whose restaurant in Veyrier-du-Lac is threatened with closure because of huge debts, said Blanc and Ducasse aggravated the dispute by pointing to the debts of his innovative restaurant.

"You don't shoot at an ambulance," he said, adding he did not want to stir up the controversy. Veyrat is negotiating with banks for a bail-out and he said remarks by Blanc and Ducasse could sour both his clientele and creditors.
Veyrat said dishes he made that were criticised as too innovative included a vegetable ravioli that omitted pasta and use of verbena sauce with a poularde fatted chicken.
"A traditional recipe in France is poularde with tarragon. Verbena doesn't taste much different, does it?" he said.
